rows.why: The internal decisions and workflows AI output drives, who the staff users are and the settings it is used in are identified and documented.
Requirements for the AI in internal workflows (accuracy needed, confidentiality, who may use it for what) are gathered from the staff and process owners who use it.
Staff are told what the AI cannot reliably do and how its output may be used and checked before it drives an internal decision.
The benefits expected from AI in each internal workflow are examined with the staff who use it, so over-reliance is weighed against what the AI really adds.
The costs of wrong output acted on in internal decisions (HR, finance, approvals, operations) are examined against the organisation's risk tolerance.
The decisions and workflows the AI may drive internally are scoped, with those it may not drive stated.
Human review of AI output before it becomes an internal decision or action is defined, assessed and documented, so staff do not over-rely on it.
The likelihood and size of harm from wrong or misused AI output in internal workflows, including insider misuse, are identified and documented.
The AI's performance is measured on the real HR, finance and approval cases it is used for, not only in generic tests.
How the AI is behaving inside internal workflows in production, including drift and unusual use by staff, is monitored.
Each internal workflow fails safely, falling back to manual handling or a hold, when the AI is wrong or beyond its knowledge limits.
Who used the AI, on what, and which decisions relied on its output are logged so internal use can be traced and accounted for.
Staff can interpret the AI output in its context, with the reasoning or basis needed to judge it before acting.
Bias in AI-driven internal decisions, such as HR and approvals, is evaluated and the results documented.
Staff and those affected by an internal decision can report problems with AI output and appeal or challenge the outcome.
Domain experts in the business function confirm that the AI is performing as intended in the internal workflow it supports.
A decision is made on whether the AI achieves its purpose in each internal workflow and whether that use should continue.
Working controls limit what the AI may do in internal decisions (business rules, limits on what output is accepted, how staff and AI share the task).
Procedures exist to respond to and recover from a decision made on wrong AI output or insider misuse once it is found.
Responsibility and a means exist to switch off or override the AI in an internal workflow when its outcomes depart from intended use.
Incidents and errors from AI-driven internal decisions are reported, tracked, communicated to those affected and reviewed.

review.reason: Why (business rules, limits on accepted output, how staff and AI share the task) repeats MAP 3.3 (scope of decisions) and MAP 3.5 (human review) in different words.
Empty cis_refs although LLM-14.9 (role-specific training) supports telling staff what the AI cannot do and how to check its output.
LLM-17.3 is a security-incident reporting process, not a way for staff or affected people to report AI output problems or appeal; weak support for this row.
HR and finance data handled through the AI (employee records, insider access) carries privacy risk that nothing in the rows examines for this area.
Bias in HR and approval decisions harms the employees or candidates affected; the area's impacts (process, data) may be too narrow.
